newsitem.title: UK: Leading economist sees no need for British tax rises.
newsitem.headline: Leading economist sees no need for British tax rises.

text.p: Strong economic growth and improving public finances mean British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown does not need to raise taxes at all in his first budget, a leading economist said on Monday.

Patrick Minford, professor of economics at Liverpool University and one of the independent advisers to Brown's Conservative predecessor, Kenneth Clarke, advised the new Labour finance minister to sit back and enjoy the buoyant economy he has inherited.
"Brown does not need the money unless he plans a most un-New-Labour-like spending binge," he said in a quarterly economic bulletin.
"My advice is enjoy your luck and claim the credit for New Labour."

In his last budget, Clarke forecast a public sector borrowing requirement of 19.2 billion pounds ($31.9 billion) for this financial year. But that was before the 1996/97 PSBR undercut its forecast by more than three billion pounds.

With latest figures also showing Britain's economy grew by an annual 3.1 percent in the first quarter of the year -- well above the 2.5 percent pencilled in to Clarke's last Red Book for the budget -- tax revenues should be higher and eat further into public debt.
"His public borrowing requirement is melting away...and at that equal to the magic figure where the ratio of public debt to national income remains about constant," Minford said.
Minford is flying in the face of prevailing opinion, as he often does.
Most economists say that unless Brown's budget includes several billion pounds of tax rises, the newly independent Bank of England will be forced to push interest rates higher and higher.
Base lending rates have already been ratcheted up, in two quarter-point notches, to 6.5 percent since Labour stormed to power on May 1.
The problem is that although a rampant pound is hurting exporters, high street spending is going through the roof.
Figures published on Monday showed consumer credit leapt by more than a billion pounds in May, while retail sales soared 5.3 percent in the year to May.
With building societies -- traditional mortgage lenders -- issuing shares worth more than 30 billion pounds to millions of members over the summer, the pace of spending is unlikely to slow.

Minford forecast robust economic growth of 3.0 percent this year but saw underlying inflation at 2.3 percent, falling to 1.9 percent next year. He thinks buoyant consumer spending will not fuel inflation.

Noting Labour's election promises to leave income tax rates untouched and not to extend the scope of value added tax, he said the spirit of those pledges meant that other income tax allowances and tax relief on home loan payments might also be left alone.
If Brown does not tamper with personal taxes to any great extent, that leaves the corporate sector. Here, he is tipped to cut or abolish advanced corporation tax (ACT).

That would hit the large pension funds and institutions which dominate Britain's stock market. They are exempt from ACT and can claim it back on their equity holdings. But no tax would mean no rebate.

Minford warned Brown not to go down that road. It would sit ill, he said, with plans to encourage people to move to funded private pensions in an attempt to reduce the huge welfare bill over the long term.

In a final stab at Brown's plans, Minford said there was no guarantee his welfare-to-work plan -- the centrepiece of the budget, funded by a windfall tax on Britain's privatised utilities -- would succeed.
Three billion pounds of the money raised will be used to offer firms rebates to take on young, long-term unemployed people -- 250,000 of them, Brown hopes.
"All the evidence from such schemes here and abroad is that they do nothing to raise employment permanently," Minford added. ($ = 0.601 British Pounds)
